demographics.trauma_type: Accidentally caused serious injury to another

Triggers.value: Physical pain in a part of the body

Threat.value: I am unable to relax even when I know I am in a safe place
I feel threatened by strangers approaching me even in ordinary situations
I watch other people closely for signs that they might harm me

Memory.value: When memories come to mind of what happened, I feel my body is in the same position as when the frightening event occurred.
When I remember the event I feel intense rage
When I remember the event I feel overwhelming grief

Negative Appraisals.value: There is something about me that made the event happen
I am no longer capable of doing the things that defined me

vignette:
Mark is a 54-year-old forester who has worked in the Pacific Northwest for over thirty years, a career that once grounded his sense of purpose and competence. Eighteen months ago, during a routine felling operation, a chain of events he still replays in vivid detail led to a tree he was directional-felling striking a younger crew member, Dan, with such force that Dan's leg was crushed below the knee. The injury required multiple surgeries and eventually an amputation. Mark was not physically hurt in the moment, but he felt the saw's recoil in his shoulders as the trunk twisted, and in the frantic minutes that followed he heaved against the fallen timber with his lower back torqued at an awkward angle. That same dull ache in his lower back has never fully left him. When it flares-bending to tie his boot, or lifting a bag of groceries-his body instinctively tenses into the same hunched, straining posture he held that afternoon, and the memory floods back with it: the sound of the saw, Dan's shout, the sickening weight of the log.

In the first weeks after the accident, Mark found himself unable to sit still at home. He would pace the living room, his jaw clenched, watching the driveway for no one in particular. His wife noticed he flinched when their dog approached from behind; he began scanning the aisles at the hardware store, cataloguing every man who walked in. He could not shake the conviction that strangers posed a latent threat, even in ordinary places like the post office or the gas station. At night, when the house was quiet, he lay rigid, his mind racing with replays of the event. What frightened him most was not the memory itself but the rage that accompanied it-a hot, wordless fury that he sometimes directed at himself, sometimes at no one at all, and that would leave him shaking. And then, just as suddenly, grief would overtake him: a heavy, sinking sorrow for Dan, for the life Dan had lost, for the fact that Mark had done it.

Mark had always believed that responsibility for a mistake meant examining your own choices. But as weeks turned into months, that belief warped into something darker. He became certain that something inside him-some flaw he could not name-had made the accident happen. He began to doubt his own judgment in small decisions, second-guessing the lean of a tree or the placement of his feet. The thought that he could no longer trust himself spread like a crack through a windshield. By the time the company offered him a desk-based role, he turned it down; he could not imagine doing any job that once defined him, because he was no longer a man who could be counted on. He stopped accepting invitations from friends, avoided the diner where he used to grab coffee with colleagues, and began driving a longer route home to bypass the stretch of forest road where the logging camp was visible.

Today, Mark arrives for his first therapy appointment with his wife waiting in the car. He has lost nearly fifteen pounds, sleeps in fits, and has not worked in six months. He came because his wife said she could not watch him disappear piece by piece, but also because a part of him, buried under the shame, still wants to believe he might again feel capable of something. What he is most afraid of-and what he does not say aloud-is that he will sit in this room and confirm what he already knows: that the accident revealed something true about him, and that there is no way back to the man he used to be.
